name: HERMES_OUTCOME_GRADER_CLOSE_CACHE_20261107
comment: ANCHOR: HERMES_OUTCOME_GRADER_CLOSE_CACHE_20261107 — daily_close_cache held an arbitrary quote
of each day instead of the last one, so every Hermes outcome graded against the close cache
was graded against a morning or intraday print.
The statement was `SELECT DISTINCT ON (UPPER(symbol), fetched_at::date) ... ORDER BY
UPPER(symbol), fetched_at::date, fetched_at DESC`. PostgreSQL resolves an unqualified ORDER BY
name against the SELECT-list output names first, and a cast is named after its argument, so the
third output column is itself called `fetched_at` and the DESC key bound to `fetched_at::date`.
EXPLAIN shows the consequence directly: `Sort Key: ((market_quotes.fetched_at)::date)` with no
second key. Inside a DISTINCT ON group that key is constant, so the DESC key did nothing and
each day's row was whichever quote the plan happened to deliver.
Measured 2026-11-07 through the application's own connection: two consecutive runs of the old
statement gave XLK 2026-11-06 = 165.265 and then 166.71 (true last quote 164.8); the cache as
written by the 10:50 ET run differed from the true last quote on 3809 of 5577 (symbol, day)
The gate pins: every quote-timestamp key in the ORDER BY is table-qualified (so it cannot bind
to the output column), the ordering ends with an id tiebreak, the day bucket is the New York
session date everywhere it appears (DISTINCT ON, inserted price_date, ORDER BY) so it does not
follow the server's TimeZone, the refresh window and the ordering agree on the column they
filter, --backfill-closes uses the same ordering, and the detector itself flags the legacy
statement (otherwise the other assertions prove nothing).
Hermetic: a recording cursor captures the SQL; no database, no network.
